brief: BofA's Global Financial Stress Index (41 gauges) rose from +0.15 to +0.20 week-on-week, the 43rd percentile of weekly gains, but that masked a swing from +0.03 Wednesday (post-election rally) to +0.17 Thursday, the largest one-day GFSI rise since Oct 10, 2025, coinciding with the Nasdaq's worst day since Covid. Japan's regional stress score jumped 0.50 to roughly 1.7 versus the US's rise of 0.06 to below 0.2, making Japan the most-stressed region by a wide margin, nine times the US. The Nikkei fell 6% Friday into a technical bear market (-20% from its June peak); Nikkei 3-month implied vol rose to 31.0 versus 19.2 for the S&P. The single most-stressed of all 41 gauges was Tibor-OIS, Japan's interbank funding spread, whose five-day move ranked above 99% of moves since 2000. BofA gives no explicit cause; linked to the BOJ's September hike, October minutes favoring a near-term hike, rising Japanese Treasury sales, and pension repatriation. Despite this, the yen rose only 50bps on the Nasdaq's worst day, undercutting Goldman's case that yen is the AI-unwind hedge. Equity stress has partly faded since, but the piece argues funding stress is stickier and warrants more attention than the VIX.
